speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I'm Dr. Agent. To help me understand your 8-month-old's feeding difficulties and abdominal distension, can you tell me when these symptoms first started and if there is any vomiting associated with them?

speaker: Patient
text: The baby has been very fussy, feeding less than usual, and the abdomen looks distended. Crying gets worse when the belly is touched.

speaker: Doctor
text: I need to know if the baby is passing stool or gas, and what the color and consistency of the last stool was. Also, has there been any bilious (green) vomiting?

speaker: Patient
text: There has not been fever, vomiting, or diarrhea like a stomach infection. The baby was born at 39 weeks without birth complications.

speaker: Doctor
text: Does the baby pass stool or gas regularly, and is the stool pale or clay-colored? Also, has the baby lost weight or failed to gain weight since birth?

speaker: Patient
text: The baby did not seem to pass stool normally and the belly swelling has become more obvious. Feeding has clearly decreased over the past few days.

speaker: Doctor
text: Is the baby passing any gas, and what color are the stools—specifically, are they pale or clay-colored? I also need to know if the baby has gained any weight since birth or if there has been significant weight loss.

speaker: Patient
text: The abdomen still looks swollen and the baby seems uncomfortable, especially in the lower abdomen.

speaker: Doctor
text: REQUEST TEST: Abdominal Ultrasound. REQUEST IMAGES. Given the abdominal distension, feeding difficulties, and lack of normal stool passage, I suspect an intestinal obstruction like Hirschsprung's disease; do you notice any rectal bleeding or a history of delayed meconium passage at birth?

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: The requested Abdominal Ultrasound and images are not available in the current data. However, existing test results indicate: Blood work (WBC, Hemoglobin, Platelets) is Normal. Abdominal X-ray shows dilated bowel segments with absence of gas in the rectum, suggesting obstruction. Barium Enema reveals a transition zone in the distal colon, compatible with Hirschsprung disease. Physical exam confirms abdominal distension and tenderness in the left lower quadrant.

speaker: Doctor
text: The imaging and blood work confirm a diagnosis of Hirschsprung disease, characterized by the transition zone in the colon and rectal gas absence. Since the clinical picture is clear, I will now proceed with the final assessment. DIAGNOSIS READY: Hirschsprung Disease.
